lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5, what goes on a cue card? (Key words, not every sentence.) Today: take part in a discussion, build on others' ideas, and present a claim with evidence and a chart.
A good discussion needs preparation: read or research the topic first and bring notes with evidence. Agree the rules: one person speaks at a time, listen to understand, and every voice matters.
Build on others' ideas: "Yes, and…", "That links to what Zara said…", "Could you explain why…?" Disagree politely, with a reason: "I see it differently, because…" At the end, sum up what was agreed.

picture.name: Zara
messages: Yes, and it could have lanterns.

lesson.text: Present a claim clearly: open with a hook, state your claim, give two or three reasons with evidence, and end by saying your claim again. Use formal language for a class talk.
A chart makes evidence easy to see. Say what it shows and point to it: "This chart shows how pupils come to school: most walk." A bar chart compares groups; a line graph shows change over time.
Speak clearly, loudly enough for the back of the room, at a steady pace. Listen: these claps are a steady pace, with a pause after a main point.
Make eye contact round the room, stand still and tall, and pause after each main point so listeners can think. Practise out loud and time yourself.

Try it in the world: discuss one question with your family, such as what your world needs next. Let each person build on the last speaker's idea. Then give a one-minute talk with a chart. Next, in grade 7: speeches and media.

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Is this a steady pace?
exercises.hint: Are the gaps even, and not too fast?
exercises.explain: True: even claps with gaps are a steady pace that listeners can follow.

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Is this speaker loud enough for the back of the room?
exercises.hint: Would someone far away hear it?
exercises.explain: False: it is very quiet. Speak up so that everyone in the room can hear.

exercises.prompt: Tilly says: "We could plant a tree." Which reply builds on her idea?
choices: Yes, and we could choose one birds like.
exercises.hint: Building on an idea means adding to it.
exercises.explain: It adds to Tilly's idea instead of leaving it behind.

exercises.prompt: Which is a good rule for a discussion?
choices: one person speaks at a time
exercises.hint: What helps everyone to be heard?
exercises.explain: Taking turns means everyone can speak and be listened to.

exercises.prompt: The chart shows how pupils come to school. Which way is the most common?
exercises.hint: Find the tallest bar.
exercises.explain: The walk bar is the tallest: 12 pupils walk.

exercises.prompt: Which chart is best to show how a puppy's height changed each month?
exercises.hint: Is it change over time?
exercises.explain: A line graph shows how something changes over time.

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Where does the speaker pause?
exercises.hint: Listen for the longer gap.
exercises.explain: The long gap after four claps is a pause after a main point, giving listeners time to think.

exercises.prompt: Zara says: "We should have a quiet reading room." Which reply disagrees politely?
choices: I see it differently, because rooms are busy.
exercises.hint: Polite disagreement gives a reason.
exercises.explain: It shows respect and gives a reason, so the discussion can go on.

exercises.prompt: Put the parts of a short talk in order.
exercises.hint: Catch attention first; end by repeating your claim.
exercises.explain: A hook, your claim, reasons with evidence, then your claim again.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: what helps listeners, and what gets in the way?
exercises.hint: What would help you follow a talk?
exercises.explain: Helps: eye contact, a steady pace, pausing after points. Gets in the way: reading every word, mumbling, turning your back.

exercises.prompt: In a discussion, listening carefully matters as much as speaking.
exercises.hint: How can you build on an idea you did not hear?
exercises.explain: True: you can only build on or answer the ideas you have listened to.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence explains a chart to listeners?
choices: This chart shows that most of us walk.
exercises.hint: Say what the chart shows.
exercises.explain: It tells the audience what to notice in the chart.

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Is this a good pace for a talk?
exercises.hint: Could listeners keep up?
exercises.explain: False: it is far too fast, with no pauses; slow down and pause after each point.

exercises.prompt: At the end of a discussion, what should the group do?
exercises.hint: What helps everyone remember the outcome?
exercises.explain: Summing up checks that everyone agrees on what was decided.

exercises.prompt: Which evidence best supports: Our school needs more bike racks?
choices: 30 pupils cycle, but there are 10 racks.
exercises.hint: Which one gives numbers that show a problem?
exercises.explain: The numbers show that there are not enough racks: strong evidence.

exercises.prompt: Oli has not spoken yet in the discussion. What could you say?
exercises.hint: Every voice matters.
exercises.explain: Inviting a quiet member in helps everyone take part.

exercises.prompt: Kit says the bus is the most popular way to school. Using the chart, how could you disagree politely?
choices: I see it differently: 12 walk, 9 take the bus.
exercises.hint: Use the chart's evidence, kindly.
exercises.explain: The chart shows 12 walk and 9 take the bus, so a polite reply with the numbers is best.

exercises.prompt: Why pause after each main point?
choices: to give listeners time to think
exercises.hint: What does a pause do for the audience?
exercises.explain: A short pause lets each point sink in before the next.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to what it does in a discussion.
exercises.hint: Which one adds to what was said?
exercises.explain: "Yes, and" builds on an idea, "I see it differently" disagrees politely, and "Could you explain why" asks for a reason.

exercises.prompt: Does it help a discussion?
items: one person speaks at a time
exercises.hint: Would it help everyone to be heard?
exercises.explain: Taking turns and bringing evidence help. Talking over people and laughing at ideas do not.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences by their job in a discussion.
items: Yes, and we could add benches.
That links to what Zara said.
I'm not sure: the field floods.
exercises.hint: Does it add to what was said, push back with a reason, or ask the speaker for more?
exercises.explain: Builds on: 'Yes, and…', 'That links to…'. Disagrees politely: 'I see it differently…', 'I'm not sure: the field floods.' Asks for a reason: 'Could you explain why?', 'What makes you think so?'

exercises.prompt: Plan a one-minute talk with a chart: put its parts in order.
items: Show the chart and say what it shows.
exercises.hint: A hook to start, then the claim, the evidence, and the claim again to end.
exercises.explain: Open with a hook, state your claim, show the chart and say what it shows (your evidence), then say your claim again so listeners remember it.

exercises.prompt: Your talk has a 10-second hook, 3 reasons of 15 seconds each, and a 5-second ending. How many seconds long is it?
exercises.hint: Work out the reasons' time first, then add the hook and the ending.
exercises.explain: 3 reasons × 15 s = 45 s. Then 45 + 10 + 5 = 60 seconds: a one-minute talk.
